query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of titanium with a subsequent controlled heat treatment to induce discrete B2 precipitate formation within the single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy will produce an inverted microstructure that improves room-temperature ductility without degrading the alloy’s high-temperature strength or irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy known for excellent high-temperature performance and theoretically predicted irradiation resistance but poor ductility at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Minor Ti doping (approximately 5–10 at%) combined with a tailored heat treatment/cooling schedule to trigger the precipitation of B2 phase within the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Room temperature for ductility testing, high-temperature (around 1600 °C) mechanical assessments, and irradiation exposures under conditions simulating reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: An ‘inverted’ two-phase microstructure characterized by a continuous BCC matrix containing discrete B2 precipitates.
generation.mechanism: Titanium promotes local chemical ordering and induces the formation of B2 precipitates. These precipitates act as sites that facilitate dislocation nucleation and mobility at room temperature, thereby enhancing ductility. Meanwhile, the continuous BCC matrix ensures that high-temperature yield strength and irradiation resistance are preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: The engineered Ti-doped alloy is expected to exhibit significantly improved room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased elongation and reduction in fracture brittleness) while retaining yield strength near that of the baseline at 1600 °C and maintaining comparable irradiation resistance.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic, single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW alloy with known high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation stability but inherently poor room-temperature ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects depend on keeping the Ti concentration low enough to avoid forming a large volume fraction of the B2 phase, which could otherwise impair high-temperature performance. The heat treatment must be optimized to induce only discrete precipitates without triggering additional deleterious phases.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti doping level and the precise heat treatment parameters remain to be determined experimentally. It is also uncertain if the induced microstructural changes impact other properties such as oxidation resistance or long-term irradiation stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one of the baseline single-phase NbMoTaW alloy and one of the Ti-doped (5–10 at%) NbMoTaW alloy subjected to a controlled heat treatment designed to form discrete B2 precipitates. Characterize the microstructure using XRD and TEM to confirm the formation of the inverted BCC+B2 microstructure.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile tests to measure ductility (elongation and fracture strain)
Irradiation tests that simulate reactor conditions to assess defect formation and swelling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped and heat-treated alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility while maintaining high-temperature yield strength and irradiation resistance comparable to the baseline, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Typically, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs), comprising a two-phase ordered B2 + BCC microstructure, exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths, but poor ductility at room temperature, limiting their engineering application. The poor ductility is attributed to the continuous matrix being the ordered B2 phase in these alloys. This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an “inverted” BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix, resulting in improved room temperature compressive ductility, while maintaining high yield strength at both room and elevated temperature.

One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ].
